mcqs.question: Why does Folder.get_size() call child.get_size() instead of checking whether each child is a File or another Folder?
options: Because every child, whether File or Folder, implements the same interface — the call is identical either way, and each implementation handles its own case
Because Folder secretly stores the total size and never actually recurses
Because Python doesn't support isinstance checks
Because folders can only ever contain files, never other folders
mcqs.explanation: Composite's whole point is that leaf and composite nodes share one interface, so the caller never needs to branch on type — each node's own get_size() implementation already knows how to handle itself. isinstance checks are entirely possible in Python; this design just avoids needing them, and folders absolutely can contain other folders.

mcqs.question: A menu system currently uses a flat list of MenuItem objects with an is_submenu boolean and manual recursive helper functions scattered across the codebase. What does switching to Composite actually fix?
options: It makes the menu render faster
It removes the need for any interface at all
It replaces scattered isinstance/boolean-branching logic with one shared interface that each node implements itself, so callers stop needing to know which kind of node they have
It prevents the menu from ever being nested more than one level deep
mcqs.explanation: The core win of Composite over a flat structure with manual type checks is eliminating repeated branching logic at every call site — each node type owns its own behavior behind a shared interface. It's not primarily about speed, it still needs an interface, and it actually makes deeper nesting easier, not harder.

mcqs.question: Why is it a problem to make every File implement add(node) as a no-op, just so File and Folder share one identical interface?
options: No-op methods are always slower than throwing an exception
It silently promises a capability — adding children — that File can never actually provide, misleading callers and hiding bugs
Python requires every class in a hierarchy to implement identical methods
It makes Folder.get_size() stop working correctly
mcqs.explanation: The problem is a false promise in the interface: callers see add() and reasonably assume it does something, when a no-op silently does nothing or a leaf throws unexpectedly. This is an interface-segregation issue, not a performance one, has nothing to do with a language requirement, and doesn't break get_size() at all.

mcqs.question: An org chart tool needs get_headcount() to work identically whether called on an individual contributor or the CEO. Which trait of Composite makes this possible without special-casing the CEO?
options: The CEO node is hardcoded to return the total company headcount
Composite requires a separate database query for every org level
get_headcount() is computed once and cached forever, regardless of hires or departures
Individual contributors and managers both implement the same interface, with a manager's implementation summing its reports recursively
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly leaf (individual contributor, returns 1) versus composite (manager, sums reports including their own count) sharing one interface — no hardcoding or special-casing needed at any level, including the CEO. There's no requirement for per-level queries, and headcount isn't a static cached value in any real system.
